replying_to: Replying to Learning mixture of neural temporal point processes for event sequence clustering
display_title: Official Review of Paper343 by Reviewer bcEp

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents a general framework (NTPP-MIX) for clustering event sequences, which can simultaneously infer NTPP and cluster assignments. The authors also propose a more flexible intensity function (FATPP) based on an attention mechanism. The learning algorithm is similar to that of variational inference for mixture models, which is general in that one can use any MLE-based TPP models. The effectiveness of the proposed method is demonstrated using synthetic and real-world datasets.
content.main_review:
Strong points.
- The task addressed here may be significant; there are a few studies on event sequence clustering.
- This paper is well-written, except for some undefined variables and typos.
- There is sufficient explanation to reproduce the experimental results.

Weak points.
- Learning algorithm based on variational inference seems not to have technical contributions.
- There are some concerns about intensity modeling.
- I am wondering if the claim about the flexibility of FATPP is valid or not.

Detailed comments.
- The idea of NTTP-MIX is a mixture model, as in (4), which is very simple,  and its learning algorithm based on variational inference is very naive. So, this framework is incremental. Also, Section 3.2 describes the general procedure of variational inference for mixture models, which is not novel except for using NTPP as the likelihood. If I am mistaken, could the authors tell me about the novelty and significance of the proposed algorithm?

- In NTPP, it is generally difficult to integrate the intensity function involved in the likelihood (2). How does FATPP handle it? If FATPP requires numerical integration, the authors should discuss its computational costs, and so on. 

- In the manuscript, the authors state that basic NTPP modules need to be flexible enough to capture diverse processes. I agree with that point; however, is it true that the prior works do not have enough flexibility. The intensity-free models (Shchur et al., 2020; Omi et al., 2019) are flexible; is it possible to use them as modules? If that is the case, what is the advantage of FATPP? Besides flexibility, can the authors point out any other advantage of the proposed method in event sequence clustering? 

- In addition, in Table 1, I am not sure if it is appropriate to compare the likelihoods for the training data because the intensity function can be made more flexible by using larger neural nets. 

Minor comments.
- The authors should define the variables: $L$ and $t_L$ in Section 2.1; $K$ in Section3.1.
- Equation (6) is evidence lower bound (ELBO); the authors would mention it.
- In line 3 of Algorithm 1, epcoh should be epoch.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper addresses the interesting problem and is well-written; however, the method is somewhat incremental, and the authors' claim is concerning (see detailed comments). Accordingly, I tend to reject it.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper343 by Reviewer bcEp

content.title: Response to Reviewer bcEp
content.comment:
Thank you for the time and thorough reviews. Here are our responses to your specific questions:
# Novelty of NTPP-MIX
Event sequence clustering applies to many scenarios but traditional clustering models fail to characterize complex real-world processes. **Our NTPP-MIX is the first neural-network-based model for multivariate event sequence clustering and outperforms previous SOTA over a large margin.** We agree that the basic idea of NTPP-MIX is conceptually simple, but the learning algorithm we proposed is technically nontrivial: 1) we have to jointly optimize the variational distribution $q(Z), q(\pi)$ with deterministic parameters for NTPP $\theta$(details in Appendix A), which is hard for the standard variational inference algorithm; 2) we introduce mini-batch training into variational EM framework for efficient training (details in Algorithm 1). Moreover, reviewer #jeQM says that the NTPP-MXI framework is theoretically sound and elegant, and views simplicity of basic idea as an advantage.
# Efficiency analysis of FATPP
Same as [1-3], FATPP uses Monte Carlo Sampling to approximate the integration term. **We add a new section in Appendix C for detailed efficiency analysis and conduct experiments to confirm it.** In short, the bottleneck of previous attention based NTPP (e.g. AMDN[4] and THP[2]) is event encoding and the bottleneck of FATPP is intensity formulation.  The overall computation complexity is $O(L^2)$ for AMDN ,THP and $O(SL^2)$ for FATPP, where $L$ is the length of the sequence and $S$ is the number of samples used to approximate the integral.  We also conduct experiments on datasets with different sizes to confirm it and show runtime plots in Appendix C.

Adding a factor of $S$ to the complexity, we can model the intensity of each mark more accurately. On the contrary, AMDN is flexible enough to model the overall intensity $\lambda(t|\mathcal{H_t}) = \sum_{u}\lambda(t, u|\mathcal{H_t})$, but assumes the probabilities of time $t$ and marker $u$ are independent. THP makes parametric assumptions about the intensity, which is not flexible enough.

In general, FATPP is more time-consuming but more suitable when you want to model each mark accurately from a micro perspective and have enough computation resources. 

# Discussion about intensity-free methods
Intensity-free models bypass the intensity function and directly model the probability distribution of next timestamp $p(t|\mathcal(H_t))$. Although they can flexibly model timestamps，when encountering multi-dimensional sequence (i.e. event sequence with marks), all of them have to make the assumption of independence between time and mark. In other words, intensity-free methods  are good at modeling  the overall intensity $\lambda(t|\mathcal{H_t}) = \sum_{u}\lambda(t, u|\mathcal{H_t})$, but assumes the conditional probability of which kinds of events to occur remains constant. Our FATPP makes no independence assumption or parametric assumption about the intensity function, which is more flexible.

All MLE-based NTPPs can be used as modules, whether it is intensity-free or intensity-based.  One can choose appropriate modules based on the prior knowledge of the data. For example, intensity-free models can be used for unvariate event sequence clustering.
 
Another advantage of using FATPP is that it gives some interpretation of clustering by accurately tracking intensity of each mark from a micro perspective (as we do in Figure 5). The attention weight used in intensity formulation can also provide some interpretation and we leave it as a future work.

display_title: Official Review of Paper343 by Reviewer mfeP

content.summary_of_the_paper: The submission proposed a Mixture of Neural Temporal Point Processes (NTPP-MIX) framework that can utilize existing NTPPs for event sequence clustering, which is trained by variational EM and stochastic gradient descent. Besides, the paper proposed a NTPP model (Fully Attentive Temporal Point Process) based on the attention mechanism.
content.main_review:
The derivation of variational EM algorithm seems solid and the construction of FATPP is rational. The major concern of the paper is the choice of hyperparameters and the experimental validation:

1. How to choose the hyperparameter $\epsilon$ in experiments that has a crucial impact on the cluster estimation? In appendix, the authors only provide the value of $\epsilon$ for each model without providing a rule for it.  For example, in an imbalanced dataset, e.g., 100 sequences in one cluster and only 2 sequences in the other one, the $\alpha_1$ will be significantly larger than $\alpha_2$, and it is prone to remove the second cluster according to the rule of updating $K$ in the paper, which results in an incorrect clustering result. If the ground-truth number of clusters is known in advance, the appropriate $\epsilon$ can be found easily, but how to specify it for the ground-truth-unknown real data?

2. If my understanding is right, the reported LL in Table 1 is training LL. However, a larger training log-likelihood is not enough to indicate FATPP contributes to the success of NTPP-MIX because FATPP can be overfitting as it is very flexible. For example, a overfitting backbone NTPP can learn quite different parameters from two sets of similar sequence data in one cluster (Bias-Variance), and then the NTPP-MIX framework will tend to divide them into two different clusters because the two sets of learned parameters are quite different, which adverse to the clustering task. 

3. If my understanding is right, the reported LL in Table 3 is training LL. The training LL is not an appropriate metric for clustering in real data. A larger training likelihood can be obtained if the backbone NTPP is more flexible and the mixture framework is prone to output more clusters, e.g., the likelihood will achieve the maximum when $K=N$ (each sequence belongs to an individual cluster), but this cannot demonstrate the framework provides the correct clustering structure in the real data. 

4. Missing baselines: Neural-HP [Mei & Eisner,2016] in Table 1; Neural-HP-Mix and THP-Mix in Table 2,3,4. 

Besides, the update of $q(\pi)$ should be E-step not M-step.
content.summary_of_the_review: The theoretical part in the paper seems solid, e.g., the derivation of inference algorithm and the construction of FATPP. However, the strategy for updating hyperparameters is not satisfied, e.g., the rule of updating $\epsilon$ and $K$; besides, the metric in experiments is inappropriate to support the main claim of the paper.

Thank you for the time and review. We are encouraged that you appreciated our theoretical part (e.g. derivation of variational EM algorithm seems solid and the construction of FATPP). The following are our responses to your questions about experiments:
# Choice of hyperparameter $\epsilon, K$ 
Actually, how to choose the minimum number of instances in one cluster (e.g. $\epsilon$) is an open problem not only for event sequence clustering [1], but also for general data [2].   In general, the choice depends on your prior knowledge about the dataset and your purpose for clustering: If you want to get clusters with small sizes for micro-level analysis, small $\epsilon$i s a good choice. As for number of clusters $K$, set a large $K$ and  Variational Bayesian mixture model has a natural tendency to set some mixture weights values close to zero and choose a suitable number of effective components automatically [3].  We also evaluate the ability to select the number of clusters in Table 4, we can see that $K$ selected by NTPP-MIX is closer to the ground truth compared with SOTA.

# Metric for event sequence modeling
In the context of clustering, our goal is to model observed data. And on real-world datasets where the ground truth labels are unknown, LL on observed data is a commonly used metric. For consistency and comparison with Section 5.2, we use LL on training set as metric. **Considering that readers may be concerned about how FATPP performs on traditional settings, we add a new section in Appendix D to test it performance for modeling unobserved data (and add two intensity-free baselines LogNormMix[5] and AMDN[4]) .** LL on testing set is shown below:

| Dataset    |   Homo | In-homo | Inhibit | Excite | In&Ex |   Stock | eCommerce | Neuron |
|------------|-------:|--------:|--------:|-------:|------:|--------:|----------:|-------:|
| RMTPP      | -23.87 |  -24.65 |  -44.30 | -41.35 | 25.66 | -102.12 |   -168.57 |  46.00 |
| THP        | -23.87 |  -24.92 |  -42.13 | -41.45 | **25.80** |  -91.92 |       N/A |  40.87 |
| SAHP       | -23.88 |  -24.61 |  -43.77 | -40.47 | 25.71 |  -94.16 |   -116.04 |  58.69 |
| LogNormMix | -23.92 |  -24.75 |  -42.64 | -40.76 | 25.51 |  -74.60 |   -122.44 |  **67.75** |
| AMDN       | -23.99 |  -25.00 |  -42.32 | -40.60 | 25.56 |  -73.07 |    **-99.76** |  64.37 |
| FATPP      | **-23.86** |  **-24.36** |  **-41.29** | **-40.43** | 25.69 |  **-68.75** |   -152.38 |  62.67 |

We can see that FATPP ranks top 1 in 5 datasets out of 8, ranks top 3 in 7 datsets. Result on this train-valid-test setting is even better than Table 1, which shows FATPP does not have serious overfitting problems. One possible reason is that the intensity formulation of FATPP models the interaction among events instead of just fitting the distribution, the learned interaction can be generalized to unseen data.  In general，Table 1 and this new table together show the flexibility of FATPP is valid.

Moreover,  two sets of different parameters of one cluster will not result in division. This is becasue that NTPP-MIX is not a two-step model that uses the learned parameters for clustering, but a joint model that jointly performs modeling and clustering. If there are two different NTPPs modeling the same cluster, then the mixing weight of one will become smaller and smaller during training and be removed in the end. 
# Metric for clustering
As an unsupervised task, we usually do not split training and testing sets for clustering. LL on observed data is a commonly used metric when the ground truth assignments are unknown [3]. Moreover,  NTPP-MIX will not over-segment data for two reasons: 1) after initialization, $K$ can only decrease but can not increase. 2) As a Variational Bayesian mixture model, NTPP-MIX has the tendency to set some mixture weights values close to zero. Experiment in Table 4 shows that NTPP-MIX has the ability to choose the appropriate number of clusters. Case study in Figure 5 shows that it can uncover real distribution of the observed data.

replying_to: Replying to Learning mixture of neural temporal point processes for event sequence clustering
display_title: Official Review of Paper343 by Reviewer jeQM

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper contains two main contributions:
1. An approach for clustering event sequences by learning a mixture of neural temporal point process (NTPP) models. 

    The clustering approach follows the lines of the Bayesian treatment of GMM in Section 10.2 of ([Bishop, 2006](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/people/cmbishop/prml-book/)). Specifically, the cluster-conditional density for each cluster $z \in \\{1, ..., K\\}$ is modeled with a separate NTPP as $p(\\{t_1, ..., t_N\\} | z) = p(\\{t_1, ..., t_N\\} | \theta_{z})$. Then, the posterior over the cluster assignments and parameters of the different NTPP models are jointly optimized by maximizing the ELBO.
2. A new NTPP model, where the conditional intensity is defined fully via self-attention. 

    Most existing NTPP models encode the event history $\mathcal{H}\_{t\_i}$ into a single vector $\mathbf{h}\_i$. In contrast, the proposed approach defines the intensity for mark $u$ at time $t$ as a function of **all** past events $\mathcal{H}\_{t\_i}$ using an attention mechanism.
content.main_review:
## Strengths
- The proposed approach is theoretically sound and elegant.
- Paper is well-structured, clearly-written, and the main ideas are easy to understand. The description of the experimental setup is very detailed, which should make the results easy to reproduce.


## Weaknesses
### 1. Efficiency of the proposed model

As far as I understand, the proposed model is computationally much more expensive than existing transformer-based NTPP approaches. This aspect is not discussed in the paper and isn't analyzed in the experiments, even though it can be important in practice. 
To explain this, let's look at how the conditional density $p(t_i | \mathcal{H}\_{t\_i}) = \lambda^*(t_i) - \int\_{t\_{i-1}}^{t\_i} \lambda^*(t) dt$ is evaluated for existing transformer-based NTPPs and the proposed model.

- AMDN ([Karishma et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.11308)):
    - we need to perform a **single forward pass** of the transformer to embed the history $\mathcal{H}_{t_i}$ into a vector $\mathbf{h}\_i$
    - we evaluate $p(t_i | \mathbf{h}\_i)$ in closed form
- In transformer Hawkes process (THP) ([Zuo et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2002.09291)) 
    - we need to perform a **single forward pass** of the transformer to embed the history $\mathcal{H}_{t_i}$ into a vector $\mathbf{h}_i$
    - we evaluate the integral $\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} \lambda^*(t) dt$ with Monte Carlo integration, which is more expensive than the previous approach
- In FATPP (this work)
    - we need to perform **multiple forward passes** of the transformer to evaluate the conditional intensity $\lambda^*(t)$ at points randomly sampled in the interval $(t_{i-1}, t_{i})$ to approximate the integral $\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i} \lambda^*(t) dt$. Of course, these can be done in parallel. However, even a small number of MC samples is used (e.g., 20), this increases the memory footprint of the model by a factor of 20.

Moreover, sampling cannot be done exactly in the FATPP model. In AMDN, we can sample the next inter-event time analytically. In THP we can use thinning since the conditional hazard decays over time (so an upper bound on the hazard is easy to obtain), which still leads to exact sampling. In contrast, FATPP would require inverse transform sampling with multiple forward passes and 2 approximations: (1) approximating the compensator with Monte Carlo and (2) inverting the compensator with numerical root-finding to obtain a sample.

At the very least, the above limitations should be mentioned in the paper. It would be even better to demonstrate the runtime / memory-consumption plots for different models on different dataset sizes. 

Please let me know if I misunderstood any aspects of the proposed model in my description above and should update my assessment.

### 2. Choice of baselines during experimental evaluation

The main motivation for the proposed FATPP model is its flexible parametrization of the intensity function. However, experiments in Section 5.1 do not compare to existing flexible NTPP models, such as FullyNN ([Omi et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.09690)), LogNormMix ([Shchur et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.12127)), or the transformer-based AMDN model ([Karishma et al., 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.11308)). The implementation of all these 3 models is publically available, so the comparison should be rather straightforward.

## Minor comments
- Another simple baseline for sequence clustering with NTPPs was proposed in Section 5.5 of ([Shchur et al., 2020](https://arxiv.org/abs/1909.12127)). The learned sequence embeddings could be clustered with K-means to assign sequences to clusters. This approach could be added to Section 5.2.
- Equation 2: $\int_0^T$ instead of $\int_0^{t_L}$ since we're talking about a TPP on $[0, T)$.
- Figure 3 is rather hard to read because of the juxtaposition of all intensity curves. It might be helpful to provide plots in the appendix, where the intensity is plotted separately for each model.
- Table 3: please elaborate the meaning of "crash" in "complex time intervals ... make RMTPP-MIX crash".
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper addresses a relevant problem. The proposed approach is simple (which is an advantage), and the presentation is very thorough and clear. My main two concerns with this work are: (1) lack of discussion of the limitations of the proposed model, especially related to efficiency, and (2) missing baselines in the event sequence modelling experiment.

content.title: Response to the rebuttal
content.comment:
Thank you for your detailed response and the additional experiments. Given these additional results, I agree with your assessment that FATPP has its advantages over existing neural TPPs, which can be useful in some contexts. Still, there are two more points that I would like to see addressed:

* One important aspect not covered by the new analysis is the memory consumption of the model. Transformer-based TPPs already struggle to process sequences with >1K events, so it would be interesting to see what maximum sequence length FATPP can handle, given that the memory complexity also goes from $O(L^2)$ to $O(SL^2)$.

* I agree with the point 3 raised by reviewer #mfeP regarding the LL metric reported in Table 3. The description of the experiments seems to imply that the LL on the training set is reported, which clearly favors a more flexible model that overfits. 

  The correct approach would be to report the LL on the validation set: That is, after fitting $q(\pi)$ and $\theta$ on the **training sequences**, you estimate the cluster assignments $q(Z)$ for the **validation sequences**, and then report $\mathbb{E}_{q(Z)} [\log p (S | Z, \theta)]$ for the validation sequences (this quantity, technically, isn't the true LL, but that's the name used in Section 5).

  If the results in Table 3 already are computed on validation data, this should be clarified in the paper.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes Mixture of Neural Temporal Point Processes (NTPP-MIX) which utilize the existing NTPPs for event sequence clustering. Similar to Xu & Zha (2017), the prior distribution of coefficients for cluster assignment is modeled by a Dirichlet distribution and the conditional probability of a sequence is modeled by the mixture of series of NTPPs. The authors introduce a variational EM algorithm coupling with Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) to train the model. Lastly, to further improve its capability, the authors also propose a fully data-driven NTPP based on the attention mechanism named Fully Attentive Temporal Point Process (FATPP).
content.main_review: First, the paper is well organized and clearly presented. However, the proposed framework is more like a "linear combination" of NTPP, clustering framework, and a standard variational learning strategy. Besides, the contribution of the proposed FATPP is also incremental comparing to other attention-based point process model.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper343 by Reviewer H6cH
display_title: Simple basic idea but performs well

content.title: Simple basic idea but performs well
content.comment:
Thanks for your time and comments. The following is our response:
1. We agree that the basic idea of our work is simple, but it works well on the task of event sequence clustering. Moreover, it is the first work that uses neural networks for event clustering and outperforms SOTA  over a large margin. Reviewer #jeQM even views simplicity as an advantage.
2. Despite the simple basic idea, it is not straightforward to use the standard variational inference for optimization: 1)our model contains probabilistic distribution $q(\pi),q(Z)$ and deterministic  parameters $\theta$ for NTPP, which makes NTPP-MIX a semi-Bayesian model which can not be optimized by standard EM. Thus, we combine SGD with variational EM to optimize $\theta$ (detailed    derivation is in Appendix A). 2) Because of the use of NTPP, we have to use mini-batch training, which also contradicts the standard EM as $q(\pi)$ is a global distribution for the whole dataset. We use an iterative way to update $q(\pi)$ (details are in Algorithm 1 and  Appendix E)
3.  We propose FATPP to further promote NTPP-MIX. Note that NTPP-MIX with existing NTPP modules (e.g. RMTPP, SAHP) has already outperformed baselines greatly. FATPP is an extension of the recent attention-based NTPPs. If we view feature extraction as ''encode'' and intensity formulation as ''decode'', most existing attention models mainly focus on ''encode'' but make strong parametric assumption for ''decode''. Our FATPP improves ''decode'' by using a flexible attention-based method, which frees the intensity from parametric assumptions. In this way, both ''encode'' and ''decode'' are fulfilled by attention (that's why we call it ''fully attentive''). Experiments  show that FATPP is more flexible than existing attention models: In Figure 3(a), FATPP is the only one that can model the smoothness; In Figure 3(c), it is the only one that models the change from inhibition to excitation.  Experiments in Sec 5.2 show it helps event sequence clustering.

content.title: General response to chair and reviewers
content.comment:
Dear area chair and reviewers,

We appreciate the reviewers' time and effort. In general, the reviewers think that our work is theoretically solid and elegant (Reviewer #jeQM, #mfeP), well-written (#H6cH, #jeQM, #bcEp), and easy to reproduce (#jeQM, #bcEp). The major concerns lie in our technical novelty (#H6cH, #bcEp), efficiency analysis (#jeQM, #bcEp) and metric choice (#mfeP, #bcEp). However, we believe there exist some misunderstandings about our work which may lead to imprecise evaluation. Before responding to specific comments, we would like to restate the background and our contributions to provide an overview of our work and response to some common issues.
# Motivation and background
 Event sequence clustering is important to many scenarios e.g. e-Commerce and electronic health. While most existing works utilize traditional temporal point processes (TPP) for clustering, which make strong parameteric assumptions and can not model the complex real-world processes. Therefore,  **multivariate (marked) event sequence clustering is a problem that has not been well solved yet.**
# Method
In this work, we propose Mixture of Neural Temporal Point Processes (NTPP-MIX) for multivariate event sequence clustering. **This is the first neural-network-based model for multivariate event sequence clustering and can utilize many existing NTPP as its modules.** 

Our NTPP-MIX is conceptionally simple but technically nontrivial. As we combine variational inference with neural networks, it is not straightforward to use the standard variational EM algorithm for training: 1) we have to jointly optimize the variational distribution $q(Z), q(\pi)$ with deterministic parameters for NTPP $\theta$; 2) we have to introduce mini-batch training into variational EM framework becasue of the use of neural networks.
# Experiments
**Experiments on synthetic and real-world benchmarks show the effectiveness of our NTPP-MIX framework against state-of-the-art methods.**  We also conduct experiments on cluster number selection, clustering stability, hyper-parameter setting, etc. to further analyze our NTPP-MIX.
